segment_name: Opening: The Boy Who Never Quite Grows Up

questions.question: Oliver, I want to start with something you flagged that genuinely surprised me. You said that line — 'No words can express the secret agony of my soul' — is almost *comic*. That it's a joke, almost. Can you defend that? Because most people read it and feel devastated.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to open with his most provocative take — that David is performing, not confessing — and immediately put Daniel and Edmund on the back foot

questions.question: Edmund, you want to read David's imagination — that passage about the 'innocent romantic boy making his imaginative world out of sordid things' — as a *moral* faculty. Almost a kind of grace. Daniel, I suspect, is about to tell you that's dangerously sentimental. Edmund, make your case first: what does imagination actually *do* for David, in your reading?
questions.intent: Get Edmund to commit fully to the moral-formation reading before Daniel dismantles it on class grounds — sets up the sharpest disagreement in the segment

questions.question: Daniel, Edmund just made a case for David's suffering as soul-building. You've got that passage from chapter thirteen — the comparison to Steerforth and Traddles still at school — and you read it very differently. What's actually happening in that moment, structurally?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to read or quote c13:p4 on the boys who stay in school, and make the 'class sorting machine' argument as sharply as possible — direct counter to Edmund

questions.question: Edmund, Daniel's basically saying the warehouse doesn't brutalise David's soul — it performs an economic function. That Murdstone isn't the villain, the *system* is. Does that reading do anything for you, or does it actually miss what Dickens cares about?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to directly rebut Daniel — ideally produces the 'moral realist vs social reformer' clash both hinted at in pre-interviews

questions.question: Here's the thing I keep coming back to, and I want all three of you on this: if David is — as Oliver argues — *performing* his own childhood for us, curating which suffering counts, does that make him unreliable? Untrustworthy, even? Or is that precisely what makes Dickens a great novelist — that he builds the unreliability right into the voice?
questions.intent: Open the final thread on narrative voice and reliability — lets all three experts synthesise their positions and sets up future segments on David as narrator

steering_notes: The productive fault line in this segment runs between Edmund's moral-formation reading, Daniel's structural-class reading, and Oliver's performativity reading — they're not just disagreeing about theme, they're disagreeing about what kind of novel this *is*. Keep pushing on that. Don't let anyone score points without the others responding. The key passage is c13:p67 — all three want to quote it and all three read it completely differently, so at some point ask them to actually read it aloud and then immediately disagree about what they just heard. The theological dimension Edmund flagged (Eden, Fall, Purgatory) is good radio if it comes up naturally but don't force it — let Daniel react to it, because he'll have something sharp to say. Watch for Oliver and Daniel finding unexpected common ground on David-as-narrator, which might leave Edmund isolated in an interesting way.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund reads c13:p67 as moral vision redeemed through suffering; Oliver reads the same passage as David *still narrating himself into being* in the present tense — ask them to fight over the words 'seem to see'

Daniel's point that the Steerforth/Traddles comparison is about class sorting directly contradicts Edmund's claim that the warehouse is about lovelessness, not economics — these two need to go head to head on what the warehouse is *for*

Oliver and Daniel may converge on David-as-unreliable-narrator (Oliver via performativity, Daniel via the political need to rewrite one's own history) in a way that isolates Edmund — worth surfacing explicitly

Edmund's 'path of flowers' to 'death-blow' reading (c6:p68 as moral injury) versus Oliver's sonic/rhythmic reading of the same passage — both want to quote it, let them quote it back to back and ask the audience to hear the difference

segment_name: The School of Hard Knocks: David's Education in Betrayal

questions.question: Edmund, I want to start with that passage in chapter six — 'God help me, I might have been improved for my whole life, I might have been made another creature perhaps, for life, by a kind word at that season.' You've called this the heart of the novel. But Oliver's been whispering in my ear before we started that this might actually be David performing his own victimhood — that the adult narrator is laying it on a bit thick. Are you buying that, or is this Dickens at his most genuinely devastating?
questions.intent: Get Edmund's strongest moral-tragedy reading on the table early, then immediately flag Oliver's counter-read to create tension before Oliver even speaks

questions.question: Oliver, you've said something that I keep turning over — that by the end of the novel David basically *is* Steerforth. Charming, isolated, uses language as a weapon. That's a genuinely dark claim. Can you walk us to that? Because Daniel is going to tell me Steerforth's charm is backed by money and class protection, and David's isn't — so where's the equivalence?
questions.intent: Draw out Oliver's strongest take about David as performer-and-predator, and simultaneously provoke Daniel's class-power objection before Daniel makes it

questions.question: Daniel, there's a boy at Creakle's school who gets named 'Exchange or Barter' out of an arithmetic textbook because he was literally traded against a coal bill. You've said that moment is 'anatomy, not sentiment.' But Edmund would say Dickens puts it in to horrify us morally — to show us a child denied recognition. Is that the same thing, or are you two actually looking at completely different novels?
questions.intent: Force the central disagreement between systemic critique and moral individualism into the open using the most concrete possible passage — c8:p51

questions.question: There's that moment in chapter seven — David sitting on his bed at Creakle's crying for 'a comfortable word from Peggotty,' surrounded by those horrible bells and placards. You've said the comedy and the desolation have to be held in tension. But how does that work in practice? Because if I'm reading that aloud I'm not sure I know whether to play it for laughs or for grief.
questions.intent: Get Oliver into the specifics of voice and performance around c7:p143, which also opens up Edmund's 'spiritual desolation' reading and Daniel's institutional-silence angle

questions.question: Daniel, you've said David survives not because the system has a conscience but because he's lucky enough to have Peggotty and Betsey *outside* it. But Oliver would say those relationships are also what teach David to perform — to keep people close but at arm's length. And Edmund would say they're what preserve his moral imagination. So what is Peggotty actually doing for David? Is she a lifeline, a toolkit, or proof that individual love can beat the machine?
questions.intent: Use Peggotty as a pressure point to make all three experts defend their core frameworks simultaneously — systemic luck, moral formation, or performed survival

steering_notes: The big fault line is Rosen versus Leigh: system versus individual will. Keep pushing both of them to be concrete — when either goes abstract, ask for the passage. Oliver is the wild card who can destabilize both: use him to interrupt whenever the Rosen-Leigh binary gets too settled. The 'Exchange or Barter' passage (c8:p51) and the 'kind word' passage (c6:p28) are the two load-bearing moments — try to get all three experts responding to each by the midpoint. Watch for Edmund going too pulpit-y and Daniel going too lecture-y; Oliver's performance angle is the corrective for both. End on Peggotty if possible — it's the one figure all three have strong but incompatible feelings about, which should generate a good closing pile-on.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's claim that David 'is' Steerforth by the end directly contradicts Edmund's reading that David preserves his moral imagination — get them facing each other on this explicitly
Daniel's insistence that Murdstone is a 'rational operator' rather than a moral failure is a direct provocation to Edmund's entire framework — the 'Exchange or Barter' question should surface this

Oliver hears the 'might have been' passage (c6:p28) as adult self-pity and performance; Edmund hears it as existential tragedy; Daniel thinks it obscures the structural question entirely — all three reads are incompatible and should be put in the same room

Edmund and Oliver both want to quote the Murdstone erasure line ('he tried to put away the notion that I had any claim upon him') but for completely different reasons — Edmund sees an act of individual will, Daniel sees a structural permission slip; flag this explicitly when the passage comes up

questions.question: Oliver, you've described Steerforth as essentially an actor — someone whose entire self *is* the performance. But here's what I keep getting stuck on: Dickens gives us that one crack in the armour, c24:p19, 'I wish with all my soul I could guide myself better.' If it's all performance, what do we do with that line? Is that just another scene, or is it something different?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to articulate the distinction between genuine feeling and the capacity to act on it — his most destabilising idea — and prime Leigh and Rosen to disagree about whether the regret is real or strategic

questions.question: Edmund, you're clearly not having the 'social predator' reading — you want Steerforth as a figure of classical tragedy, a man of real gifts undone by a will he can't govern. But Daniel is going to argue that framing is a trap, that calling it tragedy is just a more sophisticated way of letting Steerforth off the hook. How do you answer that?
questions.intent: Force Leigh to defend the tragedy reading against the class-power reading before Rosen has even made his case — gets the core disagreement on the table early and lets Rosen sharpen his response

questions.question: Daniel, read us the passage — c23:p113, the 'brilliant game played for the excitement of the moment' speech. Because I want to hear it out loud before I ask you this: you say David, even as the narrator looking back, still can't quite name what happened as predation. He calls it a game, a lie. Why can't he say it plainly, even decades later?
questions.intent: Get Rosen to perform his strongest reading on the passage itself and push him toward the question of David's complicity — which will bring Leigh back in, since Leigh also wants to talk about David's blindness as the novel's real subject

questions.question: Oliver, you mentioned that the boat scene — c23:p147-148, Em'ly laughing until the boat rings — is Dickens actually writing music into the prose to show us why the spell works. Can you say more about that? Because I want to know whether you think Steerforth *knows* he's doing it, or whether he's as caught up in it as everyone else.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read or closely quote the boat passage and articulate the 'simultaneously present and self-interested' idea — his most original contribution — which will give Leigh and Rosen a concrete moment to agree or fight over

questions.question: Let's go to Mrs Steerforth — c34:p117, 'all that I had ever seen in him of an unyielding, wilful spirit, I saw in her.' All three of you want to use this passage but for completely different reasons. Daniel, you say she's not the cause of his corruption, she's the guarantor of it — she's the whole class system in one drawing room. Edmund thinks she proves character is inheritance and constitution. Oliver thinks the charm literally *is* the pathology, passed down like a family heirloom. Who's right?
questions.intent: Use the shared passage as a collision point — the same text, three genuinely different readings — and let the experts argue directly about causation: is this psychology, class, or something more like fate

steering_notes: The productive fault line here runs between Leigh's tragic-individual reading and Rosen's structural reading, with Trevelyan's performance-theory sitting interestingly between them — sometimes supporting Leigh (the regret is genuine feeling), sometimes supporting Rosen (feeling without consequence is just another form of power). Push hard on whether David's retrospective narration is itself part of the problem: all three experts gesture at this but none fully owns it. If energy flags, return to concrete passages — the boat scene and the Mrs Steerforth moment are both vivid enough to restart argument. Avoid letting this become a debate about whether Steerforth is sympathetic; that's the wrong frame. The better question is whether Dickens understood his own novel's radicalism.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh and Rosen both want to quote 'I wish with all my soul I could guide myself better' but read it in opposite directions — Leigh as evidence of genuine tragic self-awareness, Rosen as strategic performance for David's benefit. Make this explicit and force them to argue over the same sentence.

Trevelyan's claim that Steerforth is 'entirely present AND entirely self-interested simultaneously' is actually a third position that neither Leigh nor Rosen has a clean answer to — Leigh's tragedy reading requires a self divided against itself, Rosen's class reading requires a self that is instrumentally calculating. Trevelyan collapses that distinction. Flag this when it emerges.

All three experts cite the Mrs Steerforth passage (c34:p117) but for incompatible reasons — use this as a set-piece moment where you read the passage aloud and ask each to say what it proves. The disagreement will be immediately audible.

Rosen's point that Em'ly's seduction should be named as predation, not romance, will likely provoke Leigh, who insists Steerforth's cruelty is thoughtless not planned — the question of whether thoughtless cruelty can still be predation is worth opening explicitly.

segment_name: Heep's Rise and the Machinery of Social Climbing

questions.question: Daniel, let's start with the passage everyone's going to quote today — 'Be umble, Uriah, says father to me, and you'll get on. It was what was always being dinned into you and me at school.' You've called this institutional pedagogy rather than personal villainy. But Dickens gives us this speech in a scene where Uriah is actively blackmailing people. Doesn't the novel make it pretty hard to keep those two things separate?
questions.intent: Get Rosen to lay out the structural argument clearly before Leigh and Trevelyan can complicate it — establish the ideological reading as the provocation the others have to respond to

questions.question: Edmund, you've said Uriah is a self-deceiver — that the mask hasn't just slipped, it's fused to his face. But Oliver's going to tell us that Uriah is actually the most clear-eyed character in the book about how the system works. Is there room for both? Can someone be a genuine self-deceiver and also be completely right about the world?
questions.intent: Force the sharpest clash between Leigh's moral-psychology reading and Trevelyan's social-critique reading — this is the central disagreement and it needs to come out early and cleanly

questions.question: Oliver, you've talked about Dickens writing Uriah's humility as theatrical performance — almost music hall, you said. Can you give us the actual stage directions? There's a physical description in c54:p45, the bit about the eyebrows and the small eyes — what does Dickens do there, and what does it tell us about where the performance ends and the man begins?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read and perform the c54:p45 passage — this is the most vivid material in the segment and needs to be heard out loud; also sets up the question of whether what we see is a mask slipping or a soul revealed

questions.question: Daniel, you've described Micawber's great denunciation — 'Villainy is the matter, baseness is the matter' — as morally convenient. That's a fairly bold thing to say about one of the most satisfying moments in the whole novel. What exactly is it letting us off the hook for?
questions.intent: Get Rosen to make the uncomfortable argument about readerly complicity — that the pleasure of Micawber's speech is ideologically suspect — and give Leigh the chance to defend the moral weight of that scene

questions.question: Edmund, final push — Uriah ends up in prison, apparently reformed, performing model-prisoner humility for the inspector. Dickens gives him the same act at the end that he had at the beginning. Does that land for you as tragedy, as irony, or as Dickens not quite knowing what to do with the character he's created?
questions.intent: Close the segment by forcing Leigh — who has the strongest investment in Dickens's moral clarity — to reckon with the ending's ambiguity; creates space for Rosen to argue the ending is the system reasserting itself, and Trevelyan to argue the performance was always the point

steering_notes: The key fault line is between Leigh's individualist-moral reading and Rosen's structural reading, with Trevelyan occupying interesting middle ground — she agrees with Rosen that Uriah is right about the system, but with Leigh that Dickens frames it theatrically rather than sympathetically. Don't let the conversation settle into two camps too early. Push Leigh and Rosen to address each other directly rather than just talking to you. The passages that need to get read aloud are c54:p45 (the eyebrow-frowning stage directions), c41:p121 (the school speech), and c54:p171 (the bitter admission that humility worked). If energy drops, ask someone whether Uriah would have made a good David Copperfield — i.e., whether the same qualities in a different class position would read as virtuous ambition rather than villainy.
cross_engagement_targets: Trevelyan argues Uriah is 'right' about the system — Leigh explicitly wants to resist this reading, calling it 'softening Dickens's harder moral insight.' This is the sharpest direct contradiction in the pre-interviews and should be surfaced by Q2 at the latest.

Rosen says Micawber's denunciation is 'morally convenient' and lets the novel off the hook; Leigh wants to quote that same Micawber speech as Dickens at his 'oratorical best.' They are reading the identical passage in almost opposite directions — make them talk to each other about it directly.

Both Trevelyan and Rosen quote c54:p171 ('Won't umbleness go down?') but for different purposes — Trevelyan hears performance cracking to reveal calculation, Rosen hears the system's logic being admitted. Ask them to work out whether that's actually a disagreement or whether Dickens is doing both things at once.

segment_name: Humbugs and Hypocrites: Dickens's Comic Arsenal

questions.question: Oliver, you've talked about the *sound* of these passages — the way the prose itself gets clogged and self-satisfied, like it's doing an impression of the Arches Court. Can you actually demonstrate that? Read us the Spenlow 'Touch the Commons' bit and show us what you mean — what does a reader do with that sentence to make the comedy land?
questions.intent: Get Oliver reading aloud and making a performance argument, which will immediately set up Rosen's counter that the laughter is part of the problem

questions.question: Daniel, I want to push you on something. Oliver just made us laugh at Spenlow — and you're essentially saying that's the trap, right? That Dickens is so good at making these men entertaining that we forget the courts keep running and keep charging fees. Is Dickens complicit in his own satire here, or is that too harsh?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to articulate the sharpest version of his 'ridicule enables survival' argument and directly implicate Trevelyan's reading

questions.question: Edmund, you've been sitting on something — because you think both of them are slightly missing the point. You said the real subject isn't corrupt systems, it's *self-deceiving men*. So here's the test case: is Spenlow lying when he says 'Touch the Commons, and down comes the country'? Or does he actually believe it? And does that distinction matter to how funny it is?
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's moral-realism argument and force a three-way disagreement about whether Spenlow is a villain, a fool, or a tragic figure

questions.question: Daniel, let's go to the fashionable penitence passage — c63:p40. You said institutional religion *manufactures* the confessions it claims to receive, that sincerity versus insincerity is almost beside the point. Edmund, I suspect, thinks Dickens is showing us how genuine contrition gets replaced by performance. Who's right — is Dickens indicting *false* religion here, or the whole system of religious certification?
questions.intent: Set up the sharpest Rosen-Leigh disagreement — systemic critique vs moral psychology — using a specific passage both have flagged

questions.question: Last one, and I want all three of you on this. Oliver, you said David is a bit of a prude in some of these passages — that the comedy is partly *on* him, not just on the hypocrites he's watching. Does that change anything? Is David a reliable comic guide, or is Dickens occasionally winking at us over David's shoulder?
questions.intent: Open up the question of narrative voice and David's own complicity or limitations as observer — a thread all three experts can pull on differently

steering_notes: The key tension to keep live is Trevelyan's aesthetic/performance reading versus Rosen's structural-political reading versus Leigh's moral-psychology reading. Don't let them settle into mutual appreciation — they genuinely disagree about whether laughter is Dickens's weapon or his weakness. Push for specific passage readings rather than general claims; the 'Touch the Commons' line is the best litmus test because all three have flagged it for different reasons. If energy dips, go back to the audio dimension: ask someone to read rather than paraphrase.
cross_engagement_targets: Trevelyan argues Dickens *loves* the grotesques as comic constructions — Rosen's response is that this affectionate laughter is precisely what neutralises the critique; put this contradiction on the table early

Leigh says these are ordinary men making small compromises; Rosen says the system *produces* this behaviour regardless of individual character — this is a genuine philosophical disagreement about agency versus structure that should be made explicit

All three quote 'Touch the Commons' but for completely different reasons: Trevelyan for its theatrical rhythm, Leigh for its delusional sincerity, Rosen for its ideological function — pointing this out directly should produce good three-way radio

Trevelyan's observation that David is 'a bit of a prude' in the penitence passage is a gift — it opens the narrator-reliability question that neither Rosen nor Leigh addressed in pre-interview, so it should catch them slightly off-guard

segment_name: The Fog of Self-Deception: Atmosphere and Moral Blindness

questions.question: Oliver, you've said these fog passages *have* to be read aloud — that on the page they're descriptions but in the voice they're confessions. Can you actually do that for us? Take us through the 'Somebody was leaning out of my bedroom window' bit from c26:p33 and show us what you mean — what does performing that sentence tell us that just reading it quietly doesn't?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read the passage aloud and demonstrate his performance thesis, which sets up the central debate about what the atmosphere is actually *doing*

questions.question: Edmund, you just heard Oliver perform that fracture — 'Somebody was leaning out of my bedroom window.' You've called this the novel's truest insight into how self-deception works. But Daniel's going to tell us this dissociation is a *class privilege* — that David gets to have a fragmented poetic self while the prisoners at Millbank just get fragmented by the system. Is that a real distinction or is Daniel smuggling politics into a moment that's about something more universal?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to engage directly with the class-privilege reading of the dissociation passage before Daniel can make it himself — provokes the core disagreement early

questions.question: Daniel, you've called the Millbank passage — c49:p4, 'The clash and glare of sundry fiery Works upon the river-side' — the moral center of this whole segment. But both Oliver and Edmund would say the center is inside David's skull, not out there on the riverbank. So make the case: why does *that* sentence, that landscape, matter more to understanding this novel than the drunken bedroom scene we just heard?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to make his strongest materialist argument and quote the Millbank passage directly — forces him to compete with the psychological readings rather than just critique them

questions.question: Edmund, you said the fog in c48 doesn't hide the coming storm — it *expresses* spiritual myopia. But Daniel's pointing at Mrs. Steerforth standing there against that lurid sky and saying the novel is actually *protecting* her, giving her this aesthetic shield, making her grief beautiful while grinding the poor into nothing off-screen. Are you two actually disagreeing about Dickens, or about whether sympathy and critique can live in the same passage?
questions.intent: Crystallise the deepest disagreement in the room — Edmund's 'sympathy as moral insight' versus Daniel's 'aesthetics as class protection' — using the c48 storm passage as the battleground

questions.question: Oliver, last one for you — and I want to put some pressure on it. You said David isn't just blind, he's *staged* his own blindness, which is darker and more active than simple self-deception. Daniel would say: yes, and that staging is only available to people with a self worth protecting. Edmund would say: yes, and that staging is the mechanism of sin. Are they both just translating your theatrical argument into their own languages? Or is there something they're both missing?
questions.intent: Give Oliver the last word on the performance thesis while letting him adjudicate the Edmund-Daniel disagreement — ideally produces a synthesis or a sharp rejection of both

steering_notes: The segment has a natural three-way tension that maps onto distinct registers: Oliver is theatrical/formal, Edmund is moral/spiritual, Daniel is political/structural. The first question should be a performance moment to warm the room and establish that these passages *sound* different from how they read — this makes Oliver's argument visceral before the debate begins. The Edmund-Daniel fault line is the richest: they agree on the importance of moral vision but mean completely different things by it. Push them toward the c48 storm and the Millbank passage as competing 'centers' of the segment — that's where the real argument lives. Avoid letting anyone retreat into pure theory; keep pulling them back to specific sentences. If Daniel gets too structural, ask him what Dickens *felt* about Millbank. If Edmund gets too providential, ask him whether Dickens would have agreed with him. If Oliver gets too theatrical, ask him what the fog *means*, not just how it sounds.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's 'staged blindness' thesis and Daniel's 'dissociation as class privilege' thesis are describing the same textual moment (c26:p33) from opposite ends — they should be made to face each other directly on that passage

Edmund's claim that atmosphere operates as *sympathy* rather than irony directly contradicts Oliver's claim that atmosphere operates as *irony toward* David's blindness — this is a productive disagreement neither seems fully aware of yet

Daniel's reading of the Millbank passage as the segment's moral center is a direct structural challenge to both Edmund and Oliver, who place the moral center inside David's consciousness — this should be staged explicitly as a competition between two locations in the novel

Edmund's Burke reference ('moral consequence is metaphysical, not material') is the sharpest possible statement of what Daniel finds most wrong with conservative readings — if Edmund says it on air, Daniel should be invited to respond immediately

segment_name: Becoming and Belonging: The Heart's True Education

questions.question: Daniel, I want to start with you and that porcupine image, because you used the word 'brutal' in our pre-interview. When David says he's been 'bristling all over with determination' and it's all come to nothing — Dickens is clearly playing it for laughs, right? But you're saying the joke is doing something darker. What's the joke actually covering up?
questions.intent: Get Rosen's sharpest provocation on the table early — the idea that the comedy masks domination — and let Oliver and Edmund respond to a reading they'll both resist

questions.question: Edmund, I know you're going to push back on that. Because you read the porcupine passage — and that whole sequence with Mrs. Strong's phrase about the 'undisciplined heart' haunting David in the night — as genuine conscience at work. But here's what I want to press you on: is David actually *learning* anything, or is he just getting very good at feeling bad about himself?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to defend the distinction between real moral growth and what Rosen would call self-exoneration — the soul's testimony versus psychological comfort

questions.question: Oliver, you've talked about hearing David's education in the *rhythm* of the prose itself — and you've said the voice shifts registers completely between the Agnes passages and the Dora obsession passages. Can you actually show us what you mean? Because I think that's where this gets interesting — if the music is doing the moral work, does it matter whether David consciously understands what he's learning?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the vocal distinction and make a case for Dickens-as-stylist over Dickens-as-moralist or Dickens-as-ideologist; the performance element will energise the segment

questions.question: Daniel, I want to bring you back in on Agnes, because you said in our chat that 'Agnes waits as the reward for male growth' — and I think Edmund and Oliver are both going to find that genuinely uncomfortable. But here's the thing: David himself says 'I knew nothing of' what Agnes felt. He admits his own ignorance. Doesn't Dickens at least flag that this peace is bought at a cost?
questions.intent: Create a three-way standoff on the Agnes question — Rosen's structural critique versus Edmund's reading of Agnes as genuine virtue versus Oliver's argument that 'knowing nothing' is actually the honest admission in the text

questions.question: Last one, and I want all three of you on this. Edmund, you said the deepest education is learning to *want the right things* — that David's heart finally becomes disciplined enough to receive genuine love. But Oliver's argued David doesn't fix his undisciplined heart, he *accepts* it. And Daniel would say the whole framework lets him off the hook. So which is it: does David change, or does he just get a better story to tell about not changing?
questions.intent: Force a three-way synthesis or explosion on the central question of the segment — change versus acceptance versus self-legitimation — strong closing energy

steering_notes: The key tension to keep live throughout is the three-way split: Oliver sees Dickens controlling meaning through voice and comedy, Edmund sees a novel about genuine moral-spiritual maturation, and Daniel sees a novel that inadvertently exposes the class and gender machinery underneath the self-improvement story. Don't let any one of these dominate too early. The porcupine passage is the best shared text because all three have strong, incompatible readings of it — return to it if the conversation gets abstract. If Edmund and Oliver start agreeing too much about David's genuine growth, redirect to Daniel's point about Dora as the one who pays for that education. If Daniel starts dominating with structural critique, ask Oliver to read something aloud — the performance angle tends to pull the conversation back to the texture of the prose.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver argues David's peace comes from *surrendering the demand* for self-mastery — Edmund argues it comes from *achieving* disciplined affection; these are directly opposed accounts of the same ending and should be put face to face

Edmund reads the 'undisciplined heart' phrase as the soul's own testimony to itself (conscience); Daniel reads it as a mechanism of self-exoneration that lets David internalize critique without changing his relationship to power — same passage, opposite function

Rosen's claim that 'the system works perfectly' for David (he becomes a successful gentleman-writer) directly contradicts Oliver's reading that the novel is *radical* for a Victorian text in refusing the idea that moral improvement can be willed; get Oliver to respond explicitly to the word 'absorbed'

All three want to quote the 'whatever contradictions and inconsistencies there were within me, as there are within so many of us' line — the shift to 'us' is read by Edmund as Christian humility, by Oliver as Dickens pivoting to moral philosophy, and by Daniel as ideological universalising that erases class difference; staging this moment as a three-way close reading could be the centrepiece of the segment
